title: How turmeric is made: boiled, sun-dried and stone-ground
summary: How turmeric goes from fresh root to powder: boiling (curing), sun-drying, polishing and grinding, and why slow, cool grinding keeps more aroma.
body:
The bright powder in your spice jar starts as a knobbly, orange-fleshed root dug out of the ground. Between the two come months of growing and a few weeks of work: boiling, drying in the sun, cleaning and grinding. Each step changes the colour, aroma and keeping quality of the turmeric you cook with.

## 1. Growing and harvest

Turmeric is a rhizome, an underground stem, of a plant in the ginger family. In India it is planted at the start of the monsoon and harvested after roughly seven to ten months, depending on the variety, once the leaves turn yellow and dry. The clumps are dug up and the soil is shaken off.

Each clump has a central, rounder **mother rhizome** (sometimes called the bulb) and the slimmer **fingers** that branch from it. The two are usually separated, because the bulbs are thicker and take longer to cook and dry.

## 2. Curing: boiling the fresh rhizomes

Fresh turmeric isn't simply dried. It is first boiled, a step called curing. The cleaned rhizomes are boiled in water until they are soft enough to pierce easily with a pointed stick or fork, and they give off a strong, characteristic turmeric smell. Some processors add a little lime or soda to the water; many use plain water.

Curing does several jobs:

- it stops the rhizome from sprouting, so it can be dried and stored;
- it cooks the starch inside, which helps the turmeric dry evenly and gives a firm, horny texture;
- it spreads the colour more evenly through the root;
- it cuts down the drying time.

Over-boiling makes the colour dull and the rhizomes brittle. Under-boiling leaves them slow to dry and uneven in colour. Getting it right is a matter of experience.

## 3. Sun-drying

The boiled rhizomes are spread out in a thin layer, on clean mats, sheets or a drying floor, and dried in the sun. They are turned regularly and covered at night or if it rains. Drying usually takes one to three weeks, depending on the weather and the thickness of the pieces.

Turmeric is dry enough to store when the fingers are hard and snap cleanly, often with a sharp, almost metallic crack, rather than bending. By then it has lost most of its water. It takes several kilograms of fresh rhizome to make one kilogram of dried turmeric.

## 4. Polishing

Dried turmeric has a rough, wrinkled skin with bits of root still attached. Many processors polish it, rubbing the fingers together by hand or tumbling them in a rotating drum, to smooth the surface and remove the scales. Polishing changes only how whole turmeric looks; done properly, nothing is added to the root.

Some polished whole turmeric sold in markets has been coated with colour to make it look brighter, and lead chromate has been reported in such coatings. That is why unusually glossy, bright whole fingers are worth questioning. Read [how to tell if turmeric powder is adulterated](/learn/how-to-tell-if-turmeric-is-adulterated/).

## 5. Grinding

Finally, the dried turmeric is ground into powder. This is where much of the aroma can be kept or lost.

Turmeric's warm, earthy smell comes from its essential oil, a mix of volatile compounds that evaporate more readily when warm. High-speed mills break the spice by impact and generate friction heat, which warms the powder as it is ground. A stone mill (in India, a chakki) turns slowly, crushing the turmeric between two stones in small lots, and runs cooler. Grinding slowly at low temperature is how more of the volatile oils and the aroma stay in the powder. Read more in [stone ground vs machine ground spices](/learn/stone-ground-vs-machine-ground-spices/).

## What curcumin is

Curcumin is the compound that gives turmeric its yellow-orange colour. Strictly, it is the main one of a small group of related pigments called curcuminoids. Labs measure curcumin content, usually as a percentage by weight, and the spice trade uses the figure as a measure of colour strength and quality.

Curcumin content varies with the variety, where and how the turmeric was grown, how it was cured and dried, and how long it has been stored. Curcumin also fades in strong light, which is one reason to keep turmeric in a closed, opaque container.

## Storing turmeric

- **Powder**: airtight, away from light, heat and moisture. Check the packed-on date and use it within a few months of opening for the best aroma.
- **Whole dried fingers**: they keep longer than powder. Grind a small amount at a time in a spice grinder, or grate them finely.
- **Fresh turmeric root**: wrap it in paper and keep it in the fridge for a couple of weeks, or freeze it.

## How HariLeaf makes its turmeric

Our turmeric is boiled, sun-cured, then slowly stone-ground at low temperature in small lots. We sell it as powder and as whole dried fingers.
